Nameplate capacity is the intended full-load sustained output of the refinery under ideal conditions. This capacity is usually associated with a design crude feed. 

Let's take for example a 100 kbd refinery designed on Arab Light Crude (ALC). For simplicity, let's just focus on the CDU (crude distillation unit). Engineers will never design without any safety margin, so let's assume they actually allowed for 10% runs above the declared max intake.

Case 1 shows you that the design max limit for each stream coming out of the CDU is 10% higher than its nameplate capacity. So in the same sense, you can technically run at 110 kbd of the ALC to hit hydraulic constraints for the CDU. 

But what if I have access to a middle distillate heavy crude like Forcados? In Case 2, I push 50% of ALC and 50% of Forcados on 100 kbd throughput. But this will violate the design max limit of the gasoil stream. This is therefore infeasible. Two ways to get around this: 
1) Turn down the refinery to 85 kbd on the feed
2) Change the blend to 85% ALC: 15% Forcados to maintain 100 kbd (shown in Case 3)

Both of the above still allows you to max gasoil but with different effects to the CDU intake.

Again, I have simplified the picture to only consider the yield element. There are hundreds of pipelines and pumps within the refinery (and don't get me started on the secondary units quality and other balances).

In summary, yes you can run above nameplate capacity but that's not necessarily and feasibly the only way to make more diesel.

China's Inflection Point Could Be Here 

(First published on Sparta's Market Outlook on 21 August, and point number 8 is already happening, with FOB premiums going up and eroding the cracking margins)

1⃣At least 8 mb of Basrah Medium and Basrah Heavy cargoes have been sold to Rongsheng and some state-owned Chinese refiners for prompt delivery, with Basrah Medium rumoured to be at CFR Dubai + sub 10$/bbl levels.

2⃣This is apparently in reaction to missing out on the eighth ADNOC tender (they probably tried to bid for cheaper cargoes but failed).

3⃣Pre-crisis, from Sparta’s rolling front month arbs, the delivered pricing of Basrah Medium spot cargoes was around $2/bbl lower than Oman cargoes into Far East. With Oman currently landing around Oct Dubai+$19/bbl, the pricing of Basrah Medium at CFR Dubai+$10/bbl sounds reasonable.

4⃣On the Saudi allocations front, the quantity allocated to China is now heard to be 14 mb, just 1-2 VLCCs higher than the last three months of 10-12 mb allocations. Zhenhua was heard to have been allocated as well, signalling the start-up of the 300 kb/d HAPCO refinery is imminent.

5⃣There was also 10 mb of Arab Medium and Arab Heavy crudes heard sold on a rare Saudi Aramco tender to Petrochina, Sinochem, Unipec and Rong Sheng for prompt loading.

6⃣Russian ESPO is heard to be sold out for October loaders, whilst Iranian offers are few and far between for the independent refiners.

7⃣As a result, traders are seeing more active inquiries from both state-owned players and independent refiners.

 8⃣This should translate to higher achievable FOB premiums, given cracking margins are still in double digits in the Asian markets even with eye-watering freight rates.

9⃣Product exports could start creeping up around October if the crude buying pattern is sustained as well. We will of course need to hear the actual refined product export quotas to confirm.

There’s one good reason oil prices have never roared quite as loudly as they could have during the Strait of Hormuz crisis: China. The People’s Republic slashed its imports of crude oil and drew from its huge stockpiles. Now, though, it’s diesel that’s in short supply, sending shockwaves through the economies of the US and Europe. Could China ride to the rescue again?

In theory, yes it could. The reason diesel is in short supply globally is because facilities that are available to refine crude oil into the preferred fuel for trucks, buses and trains are already running at full tilt. Many Russian refineries, formerly outsized producers of diesel, have been taken offline owing to attacks by Ukraine.

China, though, has ample spare capacity. Even before the US began its war with Iran, China had more refineries than it needed to supply its own domestic needs of oil-derived products. Its cuts to crude imports and product exports have left many plants half idle; in aggregate the 13mn barrels a day they are producing is 2.3mn barrels fewer than last February, WoodMackenzie estimates.

Long queues have formed at petrol stations around Tehran as the US blockade triggers fuel shortages and spreads alarm among motorists in a sign of the war’s growing strain on the Iranian economy.

The rush comes as Donald Trump’s administration outlined a new campaign of what it called “economic warfare” against Tehran, which the Energy Optimisation Organisation — an Iranian state body tasked with managing fuel resources — warned is facing a “critical” shortfall of petrol.

One petrol station attendant in the capital reported that people were rushing to fill up “even before their tanks are empty because they worry that the war might start over again or that prices will rise”. A limit of 20 litres per car meant that motorists had to keep returning, said the attendant, who did not want to be named.
